title: perf and flame graphs
summary: How Linux perf samples call stacks, how folded stacks become a flame graph, how to read widths and plateaus, and why frame pointers, DWARF and symbols decide whether the picture is true.
outcomes: Explain why timed sampling at 99 Hz beats tracing for CPU profiling, and estimate the error from a sample count
Fold perf script stacks by hand and compute self and total (children) shares
Read a flame graph: width, top edges, alphabetical x-axis, and functions split across callers
Diagnose broken stacks and choose between frame pointers, --call-graph dwarf and lbr
Run an end-to-end perf flame graph workflow and name what a CPU profile cannot show

lessons.title: Why profilers sample stacks instead of timing every call

blocks.md:
Your image tool takes 10 seconds and you want it faster. You could guess which function is slow, but guesses are often wrong. You could add a timer around every function, but that is **tracing**: it costs work on every call, so a function called millions of times gets slower just because you are watching it, and the result is distorted.

Brendan Gregg hit exactly this when he invented flame graphs in 2011: function tracing of a MySQL server was too expensive and perturbed the target, so he switched to **timed sampling**.

**Sampling** means: each CPU is interrupted a fixed number of times per second (by a timer, or by perf's default cycles counter tuned to fire at that rate), and at each interrupt the kernel records what that CPU was running, including the full **stack trace** (the current function plus the chain of callers that led to it). Nothing runs on ordinary function calls, so the overhead depends on the sample rate, not on how busy the program is.

If a function appears in 30% of samples, it was on the CPU (or was an ancestor of what was on the CPU) roughly 30% of the time. What sampling cannot tell you is how many times a function was called.

blocks.code:
# profile one command, 99 samples per second, with call stacks
perf record -F 99 -g -- ./imgproc in.png out.png

# or: every CPU in the system (-a) for 30 seconds
perf record -F 99 -a -g -- sleep 30

# summarize perf.data as text
perf report --stdio
blocks.caption: Linux perf: -F sets the sample frequency in Hz, -g records call graphs, and the samples land in a file called perf.data.

blocks.title: What happens on one perf sample

scenes.caption: About every 1/99 of a second the timer on this CPU fires and interrupts whatever is running, here a thread inside convolve().
The kernel reads the instruction pointer, then walks the stack to collect the chain of return addresses. This walk is what -g turns on.
The sample (pid, tid, time, CPU, addresses) is written into a per-CPU memory buffer shared with user space. The interrupted thread then resumes.
The perf record process drains the buffer and appends raw records to perf.data. Addresses are not turned into names yet; that happens later in perf report or perf script.

blocks.md: How often to sample? `-F 99` asks for 99 samples per second per CPU. If you give no `-F` or `-c`, current perf defaults to 4000 Hz (set in its source, `builtin-record.c`). The kernel caps the rate at the `kernel.perf_event_max_sample_rate` sysctl, and if sample handling uses more CPU than `kernel.perf_cpu_time_max_percent` allows, it lowers the rate itself.

blocks.prompt: Gregg's examples use 99 Hz, not 100 Hz. A background job runs for 2 ms at the start of every 10 ms tick, so it really uses 20% of a CPU. What could a 100 Hz profiler report for it?
blocks.reveal: Anything from 0% to 100%. A 100 Hz sampler fires every 10 ms, exactly in step with the job, so every sample lands at the same phase of the job's cycle: always inside the 2 ms burst, or always outside it. At 99 Hz the sample phase drifts a little each period and sweeps across the whole cycle, so the estimate lands near the true 20%.

blocks.title: Lockstep sampling: 30 s of a job busy 2 ms of every 10 ms

scenes.caption: The truth: the job is busy 2 ms out of every 10 ms, which is 20% of one CPU.
At 100 Hz all 3000 samples hit the same phase. Starting 0.5 ms into the cycle, every sample sees the job (100%); starting at 5 ms, none do (0%).
At 99 Hz the 2970 samples drift across the cycle: 570 and 600 hits give 19.2% and 20.2%, close to the truth either way. Simplified model: real timers also jitter.

blocks.md: A profile is a statistical estimate, so small shares need enough samples. If a function's true share is $p$ and you take $n$ independent samples, the measured share has a standard error of about $\sqrt{p(1-p)/n}$. A 95% margin is roughly twice that.

blocks.caption: Normal approximation to the binomial. Example: p = 0.10 and n = 990 samples (99 Hz for 10 s on one busy CPU) gives about 1.9 percentage points.

blocks.title: How many samples do you need?

scenes.caption: A function at 10%: with 990 samples the margin is about 1.9 points; with 2970 (30 s) it is about 1.1.
A 2% function is easier to pin down in absolute terms (0.9 points at 990 samples) but that is still almost half its size.
The worst case is p = 0.5: about 3.1 points at 990 samples. Quadrupling n only halves the margin.

blocks.md: A sampling profiler answers one question: what fraction of CPU samples had this function on the stack? It is cheap because work happens per sample, not per call, and it is approximate because it is a sample.

Raising the frequency is not free. Every sample means an interrupt, a stack walk and a record written to disk. Gregg suggests going up toward 997 Hz only when you need finer resolution, for example to catch short bursts.

blocks.question: You profile with `perf record -F 99 -a -g -- sleep 10` on an 8-CPU machine where every CPU is busy. Roughly how many samples do you get?
blocks.explain: -F is per CPU and -a samples all CPUs: 99 x 10 s x 8 CPUs = 7920. 990 would be one CPU. 320,000 is what perf's 4000 Hz default would give on all 8 CPUs.

blocks.question: A teammate says: 'The profile shows parse_header in 0.4% of 990 samples, so it costs 0.4% of runtime, and the call count must be small.' What is wrong?
options: Nothing, both conclusions follow from the profile
Sampling overcounts short functions, so the real share is lower
0.4% of 990 is about 4 samples, so the share is very uncertain, and sampling says nothing about call counts
perf only samples the main thread, so the share is wrong
blocks.explain: Four samples give a very rough estimate (the margin is about as large as the value), and a sampler never sees calls, only which code was on the CPU when the timer fired. A function could be called a million times and still appear rarely if each call is tiny.

blocks.md: `perf.data` is a binary file of raw samples. Two commands read it. `perf report` builds an interactive or text tree. `perf script` prints every sample as text: a header line with the command name, pid, CPU, timestamp and event, then one line per stack frame with the address, symbol and the binary it came from, **leaf first** (the running function at the top, its callers below).

blocks.code:
imgproc 4211 [002] 5123.456789: cpu-clock:
        5555555551a9 convolve (/home/u/imgproc)
        555555555312 blur (/home/u/imgproc)
        555555555488 process (/home/u/imgproc)
        555555555601 main (/home/u/imgproc)
        7ffff7c29d90 __libc_start_call_main (/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libc.so.6)

imgproc 4211 [002] 5123.466890: cpu-clock:
        555555555a77 inflate (/home/u/imgproc)
        ...
blocks.caption: Simplified perf script output for two samples of our toy program. Real output also has the sample period and symbol offsets like +0x29.

blocks.md: Thousands of these blocks are unreadable, but most of them are identical. **Folding** (also called collapsing) turns each sample into one line: reverse the frames so the root comes first, join them with semicolons, and count how many samples had exactly that stack. This is what `stackcollapse-perf.pl` from Gregg's FlameGraph repository does, and it strips offsets so `convolve+0x29` and `convolve+0x31` merge.

blocks.title: Folding four samples by hand

scenes.caption: Sample 1 arrives leaf first: convolve, blur, process, main.
Reversing puts the root first, so the line reads like a path from main to the running function.
First time we see this path: its count becomes 1. (Keys are shortened to their last frame in this trace.)
Sample 2 is a different stack (inflate under decode_png), so it gets its own line.
Sample 3 has exactly the same stack as sample 1, so only the count changes. This is where the compression comes from.
Sample 4 stops in blur itself (blur was running, not one of its callees). That is a shorter, separate path.
Output is sorted, one line per distinct stack with its count. flamegraph.pl reads exactly this format.

blocks.md: Here is the full folded profile we will use for the rest of the course: 990 samples, which is 10 seconds at 99 Hz on one busy CPU. (A made-up but internally consistent example; real programs also show libc and kernel frames below `main`.)

blocks.caption: Folded stacks: a semicolon-separated path, a space, and a sample count. Six lines replace 990 multi-line samples.

blocks.md: Two numbers matter for any function. **Self** samples: the function was the leaf, actually executing. **Total** (perf report calls it **Children**, and enables it by default when call graphs were recorded): the function was anywhere on the stack, so its own work plus everything it called. From the folded file, convolve has self = 396 + 99 = 495 (50%). blur has self = 20 (2%) but total = 20 + 396 = 416 (42%).

blocks.title: Self versus total for each function (990 samples)

scenes.caption: Self: where the CPU was actually executing. Only leaf functions score, and the self column always sums to 100%.
Total (Children): every function on the path gets credit. main is 100% because it is under every sample, and process is 52% even though it never executes code itself.

blocks.prompt: Add up the Total column for every function in this profile (including imgproc). Will it equal 100%?
blocks.reveal: No, it is far above 100%. Each sample credits every function on its stack, so one sample counts toward 4 or 5 functions at once. Here the totals sum to 488%. The perf report documentation warns about exactly this: only the Self column sums to 100%.

blocks.md: Folded files are plain text, so you can filter them with grep before drawing. Gregg's own examples: `grep -v cpu_idle` to drop idle time, or `grep ext4` to graph only file-system paths.
In `perf report`, a high Children value does not mean the function is doing the work. main is 100% in every program. Sort by Self to find what executes, by Children to find which caller to change.

blocks.question: A folded file contains `app;main;run;parse 40` and `app;main;run 10`. What are the self and total sample counts of `run`?
options: self 50, total 50
self 10, total 50
self 0, total 50
self 10, total 10
blocks.explain: run is the leaf only in the second line, so self = 10. It appears on the stack in both lines, so total = 40 + 10 = 50.

blocks.question: Why does stackcollapse-perf.pl strip offsets like +0x29 from each frame?
options: To make the output file smaller on disk
Because perf records the wrong offsets
Because flamegraph.pl cannot parse hexadecimal
So samples at different instructions in the same function merge into one stack line
blocks.explain: Two samples in convolve usually hit different instructions. With offsets kept they would be different stacks and the graph would split one function into many slivers. The script's header says offsets are stripped and identical stacks are coalesced with their counts summed.

lessons.title: Reading a flame graph: width, top edges and plateaus

blocks.md:
A **flame graph** draws the folded stacks as stacked boxes. Gregg's definition is precise and worth memorizing:

- Each box is one stack frame (one function at one position in a stack).
- The y-axis is stack depth, counting from zero at the bottom. A box's parent (caller) is directly below it.
- The x-axis is the **sample population**, sorted alphabetically. It is **not** time.
- A box's width is the number of samples that contain it. The top edge is what was running on the CPU.

blocks.title: Building the flame graph from 990 folded samples

scenes.caption: Every sample starts at imgproc (the process name stackcollapse adds) and then main, so both span all 990 samples.
Depth 2: main's children, sorted alphabetically. load_image covers 396 samples (40%), process 515 (52%), save_image 79 (8%). Each child sits on top of its parent and is never wider.
Depths 3 and 4 complete the picture. Adjacent lines of the sorted folded file that share a prefix merge into one wide box, which is why sorting matters.
Look along the top edges. The widest exposed top edge is convolve under blur: 396 samples, 40% of all CPU time spent executing that one path.
blur is 416 wide but only 20 samples of it (the left sliver) are exposed at the top; the rest is time inside convolve. Exposed top edge equals self time.
Searching for convolve highlights both towers: 396 + 99 = 495 samples, 50%. The same function under different callers is drawn twice; search adds them up.

blocks.prompt: In the graph, blur is drawn to the left of sharpen. Does that mean blur ran first?
blocks.reveal: No. Left to right is alphabetical order of the folded stacks (b comes before s), chosen because it maximizes merging of identical frames. The original flamegraph.pl simply runs `sort` on the folded lines. The time order of samples is thrown away. A **flame chart**, introduced in Chrome's developer tools, is the time-ordered cousin: x is time and nothing is merged.

blocks.md:
How to read one, in order:

1. Scan the top edges for wide **plateaus**: functions that were executing for a large share of samples. Here: convolve (40%), inflate (30%).
2. Walk down from a plateau to find the code path, and decide where to fix it. Make convolve faster, or have blur call it less.
3. Compare widths of siblings to see which branch of the program dominates: process (52%) versus load_image (40%).
4. Use search to total a function that appears under several callers.
The width in pixels is just a scaled sample count. flamegraph.pl draws on a 1200 pixel canvas with 10 pixels of padding on each side, so 1180 pixels represent all samples.

blocks.caption: The left convolve tower is 472 px wide; the one under sharpen is 99/990 x 1180 = 118 px. Frames narrower than --minwidth (default 0.1 px) are omitted.

blocks.md: Colors carry no meaning in a default CPU flame graph. Gregg picks random warm colors only to separate neighbors. Other palettes exist (for example coloring kernel, user and JIT frames differently), but never read hotness from hue.
A wide box does not mean each call is slow. It may be cheap but called very often. The flame graph cannot tell the difference because sampling never sees call counts.

Variants you will meet: an **icicle graph** is the same picture upside down (root at the top; `flamegraph.pl --inverted`), and many tools default to it. A **differential flame graph** compares two folded profiles and colors frames red where samples grew and blue where they shrank, which is useful for regression testing. All of them keep the same rule: width is sample count.
Look for the widest top edges. Width is share of samples, y is ancestry, x order is alphabetical, and color is decoration.

blocks.question: In a flame graph, `json_encode` is 300 px wide but the boxes on top of it cover 290 px. What does that tell you?
options: json_encode itself is the hot spot; optimize its loop
json_encode was called 300 times
Almost all of json_encode's time is in the functions it calls; it executes very little itself
json_encode ran during the first quarter of the profile
blocks.explain: Only the exposed top edge (10 px) is self time. The other 290 px belong to its callees. Width says nothing about call counts, and x position says nothing about when.

blocks.question: A thread profile shows `hash_lookup` as a 5% tower under `parse` and a 25% tower under `index`, and nowhere else. What share of samples include hash_lookup?
options: 25%, take the widest tower
15%, the average
You cannot tell without the call count
blocks.explain: The same function under different callers appears as separate towers. Since no stack can contain both (they are disjoint paths here), the shares add: 5% + 25% = 30%, which is what the search feature reports.

lessons.title: Broken stacks: frame pointers, DWARF, LBR and symbols

blocks.md: A flame graph is only as good as its stacks. To record one, the kernel must find every caller of the running function at interrupt time, cheaply. For user code, `perf record -g` uses the **frame pointer** method by default (`--call-graph fp`). The other choices are `dwarf` and `lbr`.

On x86-64, a function compiled with a frame pointer starts with a two-instruction **prologue**: push the caller's `rbp` register onto the stack, then point `rbp` at that saved slot. The `call` instruction has already pushed the **return address** just above it. So every frame holds a pointer to the previous frame, forming a linked list through the stack.

blocks.code:
convolve:
    push rbp          ; save caller's frame pointer
    mov  rbp, rsp     ; rbp now points at that saved value
    ...               ; body; [rbp+8] holds the return address
    pop  rbp
    ret
blocks.caption: x86-64 prologue and epilogue with frame pointers (Intel syntax). The unwinder needs only rbp: the saved rbp at [rbp] and the return address at [rbp+8].

blocks.title: Walking the frame pointer chain (simplified stack, low addresses left)

scenes.caption: Sampled inside convolve. rbp points at slot 1, which holds blur's saved rbp (@4). Slot 2 is the return address into blur. Walk so far: convolve.
Read [rbp+8] to get the caller (blur), then follow rbp to slot 4. Each step is two memory reads, which is why fp unwinding is cheap enough to run in the interrupt.
Repeat: process, then main, then libc. A saved rbp of 0 ends the chain. Full stack: convolve, blur, process, main, libc.
Now convolve is a leaf built without a frame. It pushes nothing, so rbp still points at blur's frame (slot 4). The walk reads slot 5 next: blur vanishes and process looks like the direct caller.
Worse: blur was built without frame pointers and used rbp as an ordinary register, here holding 0x2a. The walk follows junk, records [unknown], and stops. main and process are lost.

blocks.md: Why would frames be missing? GCC turns on `-fomit-frame-pointer` at `-O1` and above (one of the flags in the levels you met in the compiler course), freeing `rbp` as a general register. Gregg traces the change to 2004, made when 32-bit x86 had very few registers, and later applied to x86-64 too. The result was two decades of broken stacks in profilers that walk frame pointers.

blocks.title: The same 990 samples with zlib built without frame pointers

scenes.caption: With frame pointers everywhere: inflate sits on decode_png and load_image, and load_image is 40% of the profile.
Simplified: zlib's inflate was compiled without frame pointers. Its 297 samples lose their ancestors and gather in a detached [unknown] tower; load_image shrinks to 10% and decode_png disappears.

blocks.md:
Three fixes, from Gregg's perf notes and the perf-record manual:

1. **Rebuild with frame pointers**: `-fno-omit-frame-pointer`, plus `-mno-omit-leaf-frame-pointer` so leaves keep them too. Fedora 38 made both flags the distribution default, and Ubuntu 24.04 LTS also turned frame pointers on. Gregg reports the cost at Netflix was usually under 1%.
2. **`--call-graph dwarf`**: at each sample, copy a chunk of the user stack (8192 bytes by default) into perf.data and unwind it later in user space with DWARF debug info. Works without recompiling, but much heavier.
3. **`--call-graph lbr`**: use Intel's Last Branch Record hardware. Cheap, but only user stacks, typically limited to 16 or 32 recent calls, and often unavailable in cloud VMs.

blocks.title: Bytes stored per sample for the user stack

scenes.caption: Frame pointer mode stores only the return addresses: 8 bytes each, so a 30-frame stack is 240 bytes.

Even at the default kernel.perf_event_max_stack of 127 frames, fp is 1016 bytes. DWARF mode copies a raw 8192-byte stack dump every sample, 8 to 34 times more data, and unwinding it later costs CPU too.

blocks.md: Stacks also need **symbols** to turn addresses into names. A stripped binary shows hex addresses; install the distribution's debug symbol packages (often named `-dbgsym` or `-debuginfo`) or keep your own builds unstripped. JIT runtimes such as the JVM or Node.js generate code at run time, so perf needs a `/tmp/perf-PID.map` file written by the runtime (and Java needs `-XX:+PreserveFramePointer` for full stacks). Finally, functions inlined at `-O2` have no frame of their own; `perf script` can recover them from debug info and does so by default (`--inline`).
Missing callers, a detached tower over [unknown], or hex instead of names are not hot spots. They are profiler blind spots. Fix frame pointers or symbols before you trust the picture.

blocks.question: A flame graph shows 25% of samples in a tower `myapp;[unknown];memcpy`, detached from the main tower. What is the most likely cause?
options: memcpy is called from an unknown thread
perf ran out of sample buffer space
memcpy was inlined
The code that called memcpy (often libc or a library) was built without frame pointers, so the walk failed
blocks.explain: A failed frame pointer walk records one junk frame as [unknown] and stops, so all those samples lose their real ancestors and pile up together. Rebuilding with frame pointers or using --call-graph dwarf restores the callers.

blocks.question: Profiling a C service you built with -O2 -fno-omit-frame-pointer. Some flame graph boxes show `process` directly calling `convolve` although the code goes through `blur`. Which extra flag addresses this?
options: -fomit-frame-pointer
-mno-omit-leaf-frame-pointer
-fno-inline
blocks.explain: Skipping exactly one caller is the leaf pattern: the leaf (convolve) did not set up a frame, so rbp still pointed at blur's frame and the walk jumped straight to blur's caller. Keeping frame pointers in leaf functions fixes it. Inlining blur into process could also hide it, but then the code would no longer go through a real blur frame.

lessons.title: A profiling workflow, its costs and its blind spots

blocks.md: Putting it together, here is the classic pipeline from Gregg's CPU flame graph page, plus the newer built-in route. `perf script report flamegraph` runs a script shipped with perf that writes an interactive HTML flame graph (using d3-flame-graph) without the Perl tools.

blocks.code:
# 1. record: 99 Hz, all CPUs, with stacks, for 60 s
perf record -F 99 -a -g -- sleep 60

# 2a. classic: fold, filter, draw
git clone https://github.com/brendangregg/FlameGraph
perf script | ./FlameGraph/stackcollapse-perf.pl > out.folded
grep -v cpu_idle out.folded | ./FlameGraph/flamegraph.pl > cpu.svg

# 2b. built in: writes flamegraph.html
perf script report flamegraph
blocks.caption: Keep out.folded around: you can grep it into several focused graphs without re-recording.

scenes.caption: Recording: the kernel samples every CPU 99 times per second and perf record writes raw addresses and stacks to perf.data.
perf script resolves symbols and prints each sample; stackcollapse-perf.pl folds them into one line per distinct stack.
flamegraph.pl sorts the folded lines, merges common prefixes and draws an interactive SVG (hover for counts, click to zoom, search).
The alternative: perf's own flamegraph report script reads perf.data directly and emits an HTML page.

blocks.md: **Permissions.** The `kernel.perf_event_paranoid` sysctl defaults to 2, which means users without the `CAP_PERFMON` capability cannot profile the kernel. You can still profile your own processes in user space; system-wide profiles with kernel stacks need root or `CAP_PERFMON`.

**Cost scales with samples.** Sampling 64 CPUs at 99 Hz for 60 s produces 99 x 64 x 60 = 380,160 samples. Forgetting `-F` and running at perf's 4000 Hz default produces 15,360,000. With `--call-graph dwarf` each of those 380,160 samples also carries an 8192-byte stack dump: about 3.1 GB of perf.data. Choose rate and unwinder deliberately.

blocks.prompt: An API's p99 latency is 200 ms. Its CPU flame graph is small and boring: no wide plateaus. Where did the time go?
blocks.reveal: Probably **off-CPU**. A CPU profile only samples threads that are running on a CPU. Time spent blocked on disk I/O, network, locks, or sleeping is invisible. Gregg covers this with separate off-CPU analysis and off-CPU flame graphs, which record why and where threads blocked instead of where they ran.

blocks.md:
Other things the flame graph will not tell you on its own:

- **When** something happened: x is alphabetical. Use a flame chart, or perf script timestamps, for time order.
- **How many calls**: sampling sees only presence on the stack.
- **Why** code is slow on the hardware (cache misses, branch mispredictions): that needs hardware counters such as `perf stat`.
- **Wall-clock time** directly: with several busy threads, sample counts can exceed elapsed time, since each CPU is sampled separately.

Comparing two flame graphs by eye is error-prone because widths are relative to each graph's own total. To check a fix, record both under the same load and diff the folded files (a differential flame graph), and make sure you have enough samples for the change to stand out from noise.
The workflow: record with a modest rate and working stacks, fold, filter, draw, read top edges, fix the widest plateau that you can change, then measure again.

blocks.question: You run `perf record -g ./server` as a normal user on a stock kernel and the flame graph has no kernel frames at all. Most likely reason?
options: perf_event_paranoid defaults to 2, which blocks kernel profiling without CAP_PERFMON
The server never makes system calls
-g only records kernel stacks when -F is given
Kernel frames are filtered by stackcollapse-perf.pl
blocks.explain: At paranoid level 2 an unprivileged user may profile their own user-space code but not the kernel. Run with CAP_PERFMON or root, or lower the sysctl on a machine you control.

blocks.question: A batch job takes 40 s of wall time. Its CPU flame graph (99 Hz, one thread) holds only 990 samples. What should you conclude?
options: The profiler dropped samples, so re-record at 4000 Hz
The job was on-CPU for about 10 s; roughly 30 s went to waiting, which needs off-CPU analysis
The job used 4 CPUs
flamegraph.pl pruned most frames below --minwidth
blocks.explain: 990 samples at 99 Hz is 10 s of on-CPU time for one thread. The remaining 30 s were spent off-CPU (blocked or sleeping), which a CPU profile cannot see. Raising the rate would not change the proportion.

blocks.question: After a fix, convolve drops from 40% to 30% of the flame graph. Which statement is safest?
options: The program is now 10% faster
convolve now takes a smaller share of on-CPU samples; measure total runtime or CPU time to know if the program got faster
convolve is now called 25% less often
Other functions got slower
blocks.explain: Widths are shares of each profile's own total. A share can drop because convolve got faster or because something else grew. Pair the flame graph with an absolute measurement (runtime, CPU seconds, sample counts at a fixed rate and duration).
